input:
The Prandtl number is a dimensionless quantity that plays a central role in the study of heat transfer, and it is defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. In other words, it provides a comparison between two fundamental transport processes that take place within a fluid: the rate at which momentum is spread through the fluid by viscous effects, and the rate at which heat is spread through the fluid by conduction.

The significance of the number can be appreciated by considering the values that it can take. When the Prandtl number has a value close to 1, the implication is that momentum and heat are transferred through the fluid at broadly comparable rates, so that neither process runs significantly ahead of the other, and the boundary layers associated with the velocity and with the temperature grow to roughly the same thickness.

When the Prandtl number is large, on the other hand, the situation is quite different: momentum is spread through the fluid much more rapidly than heat, and as a consequence the velocity boundary layer becomes considerably thicker than the thermal boundary layer, while the temperature variations are confined to a relatively thin region close to the surface of the wall.

It is also worth emphasising that the Prandtl number is a property of the fluid itself, determined entirely by the physical properties of the material, and that it does not depend on the dimensions of the equipment in which the fluid is flowing or on the speed at which the flow takes place.
target:
The Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. Momentum diffusivity measures how fast momentum spreads through a fluid by viscous action; thermal diffusivity measures how fast heat spreads through the fluid by conduction. The Prandtl number compares the two rates of spreading, and its size states how the velocity field and the temperature field of a flow stand in relation to each other.

A value near 1 means that momentum and heat spread at comparable rates. Neither field outruns the other: a disturbance in the velocity reaches about as far, in the same time, as a disturbance in the temperature, and the velocity boundary layer and the thermal boundary layer grow to about the same thickness.

A large value means that momentum spreads much faster than heat. Momentum reaches well beyond the region that conduction has warmed or cooled, and the velocity boundary layer is much thicker than the thermal boundary layer. Heat transfer in such a fluid is confined to a thin layer near the wall, across which the temperature changes from the wall value to the value in the moving stream outside.

The number is a property of the fluid, formed from its properties alone, and it states nothing about the size of the apparatus or the speed of the flow: the same fluid at the same state has the same Prandtl number in a pipe of any diameter.
